questions.stem: The condition number $\kappa(A)$ of a matrix measures:

options.text: How sensitive the solution $x$ of $Ax = b$ is to perturbations in $b$ or $A$.
options.explanation: Roughly: $\kappa(A) = \|A\|\|A^{-1}\|$. If $\kappa(A) \approx 10^k$, you lose about $k$ digits of accuracy. Ill-conditioned matrices ($\kappa \gg 1$) make linear systems numerically unreliable.

The determinant is not a reliable indicator of conditioning. A matrix with very small determinant may be well-conditioned (e.g., $10^{-100}$ times the identity), and a unit determinant does not imply good conditioning.

options.text: The number of non-zero eigenvalues of $A$.
options.explanation: The rank (number of non-zero eigenvalues for symmetric matrices) is a different concept. A full-rank matrix can still be ill-conditioned.

options.text: Whether the matrix is positive definite.
options.explanation: Positive definiteness (all eigenvalues positive) is unrelated to the condition number. A positive definite matrix can be very ill-conditioned.

questions.stem: The SVD $A = U\Sigma V^T$ of a matrix is used in low-rank approximation because:

options.text: The best rank-$k$ approximation of $A$ in the spectral (or Frobenius) norm is obtained by keeping only the $k$ largest singular values.
options.explanation: The Eckart-Young theorem: the best rank-$k$ approximation is $A_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^T$ using the top $k$ singular values and corresponding singular vectors.

options.text: The SVD gives the eigenvalues of $A$.
options.explanation: Singular values are not the same as eigenvalues except for symmetric positive definite matrices. The SVD and eigendecomposition are related but distinct.

options.text: SVD can only be computed for square matrices.
options.explanation: Every $m \times n$ matrix has an SVD, square or not. This is one advantage of SVD over eigendecomposition (which requires a square matrix).

options.text: It is equivalent to Gaussian elimination.
options.explanation: Gaussian elimination solves linear systems via LU factorisation. SVD is a completely different decomposition, more computationally expensive but numerically more stable.

questions.stem: Stiff ODEs require implicit methods because:

options.text: Explicit methods require impractically small step sizes to remain stable when the ODE has components with very different timescales.
options.explanation: Stiffness arises when the ODE has fast-decaying transients alongside slow dynamics. Explicit methods have stability regions that require $h \lesssim 1/\lambda_{\max}$; if $\lambda_{\max}$ is large, $h$ must be tiny even if the solution itself is smooth.

options.text: Stiff ODEs have no analytic solutions.
options.explanation: Many stiff ODEs have closed-form solutions. Stiffness is a numerical property (related to the eigenvalue spread of the Jacobian), not a property of solvability.

options.text: Implicit methods always give more accurate solutions.
options.explanation: Implicit methods are not uniformly more accurate — they are more stable for stiff problems. For non-stiff ODEs, explicit methods like RK4 are often more efficient.

options.text: Explicit methods cannot solve ODEs with discontinuous forcing.
options.explanation: Discontinuous forcing is a separate issue. Stiffness is about the magnitude of eigenvalues of the Jacobian, not discontinuities.
